topics.topic: Drill 9 read aloud, items 1-20, page 58 - each student taking a numbered word while she corrects pronunciation in real time. The teaching content is not the words but the READING RULES she pulled out of them: a letter carrying sukuun starts a new syllable, so a ba with fatha followed by a yaa cannot be read as one run-on 'ba-ee'; the dot placement under a letter is what makes it jiim rather than another shape, and the tashkiil should be shifted slightly to the RIGHT of the letter it belongs to; waaw is a CONSONANT when it opens a word and a long VOWEL when it follows a consonant inside one, which she drew out of a single word containing both; and a long vowel is held while a short vowel is quick. She closed the drill by telling them to start reading WITHOUT the vowel marks - 'now the fatha was an indication to the ya, and hopefully in the future you would not even need the fatha' - which is the direction the course is moving

Drill 10 AT THE BOARD - students writing the words while the class listens to the audio and decides what tashkiil has to be added. This is the writing-production half of the same skill and the part that cannot be practised from the book alone. Recurring corrections: several words accept MORE THAN ONE correct marking (she said a word 'you could write it with just the [one] or with just the [other]... and you could do three options'), a word with full long vowels needs NO tashkiil at all because the vowels are already there, and the daal must be distinguished from the raa by the direction of the tail - a student wrote one for the other twice

Drill 11, which is where the one genuinely new PHONOLOGICAL rule of the hour appeared: when a kasra sits under the letter FOLLOWING an alif, the alif's vowel shifts from an 'aa' toward an 'e' sound. She generalised it - 'every time you see the kasra sound on the letter coming after alif' - and said the un-shifted pronunciation is not WRONG, just not how natives say it and still understandable. Also covered here: bayt / bayti, where the final yaa (not the taa marbuuta) is what marks 'my'; and again the point that a word can be marked several different legitimate ways and still read identically

ORAL VOCABULARY REVIEW, hands up, she calls on people - the most exam-like segment of the hour and entirely off the page. Items she pulled: hijab (veil); 'I live in my house' built from askun + fii + bayti, with both askun fii bayti and ana askun fii bayti accepted; homework in fuSHa versus the Shami word, and turning it into 'my homework' by possessive suffix; kitaab / kitaabi / your-book masculine versus feminine; the register of Habiibi and Habiibati and the social rule that it is not used with a friend of the opposite sex, only a fiance or someone you are serious about; and a long run through the acceptable answers to 'how are you' (al-Hamdu lillah, maashi, ana jayyid with the feminine form required of the women in the room, bi-khayr specifically as the GREETING answer versus khayr / al-khayr as 'good' in general, and the negative built on 'lastu' plus an adjective), plus the Shami pair mniiH / mniiHa. She also taught the demonstratives haadha / haadhihi and the nominal sentence with NO verb 'to be' - 'we don't have is in Arabic'

Page 56 picture task (reading the Toyota logo as Arabic script rather than recognising it as a logo) and then PAIR CONVERSATION setup - students pick a partner, build a short dialogue from memory, and perform it in front of the class while the rest of the class has to understand it. She was explicit that the audience is doing work too: 'I want to also make sure the students do that. So, when we speak, we are understandable to others.' The hour ran out during preparation, so the performances themselves have not happened yet and are presumably first business on Tuesday

announcements.text: SHE DOES NOT TRACK WHICH DRILLS THE CLASS HAS DONE - THE CLASS IS THE RECORD. She opened by asking them to confirm, drill by drill, what had already been covered: 'because every class we make different progress. In this class, I remember we did drill one and drill 2, correct? Can you just confirm drill one and drill 2 with unit 3?... did we do drill 4?... Then I'm assuming we read drill 6, drill 7 and eight, did we do those? We did not read 9, right?' Confirmed done before today: unit 3 drills 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. Done today: 9, 10, 11. Her two sections are at different points, so nothing about pace can be inferred from anyone else's section.

THE DIVISION OF LABOUR SHE STATED OUTRIGHT: class time is for CORRECTION, homework is done alone. 'Because I want to make sure I give you the correct answers. So we're going to do the correction in class and you do your homework on your own.' This is the answer to what in-class drill work is for - the drills done aloud in class are the answer key being delivered, which means missing a class means missing the key rather than missing a lecture.

PRONUNCIATION OF haadha / haadhihi IS GETTING DEDICATED TIME, and she justified it with an unusually candid admission about how far the problem travels: 'I have students in 201 until now they don't know how to pronounce Hada and Hadi. OK, so I'm gonna spend some time in on the pronunciation.' She then drilled it call-and-response with the whole class. Not framed as a test item, but it is the one thing she said she would deliberately spend future class time on.

THE PAIR CONVERSATION IS UNFINISHED BUSINESS. She set it up with about four minutes left - pick a partner, build a dialogue from memory, perform it in front of the class - and the recording ends with students still preparing. 'It has to be from memory, but if you wanna glance like really quick, that's fine.' No performances happened. If this resumes on Tuesday it is a speaking task Parker should have a dialogue ready for; she did not say it would resume, so this is read off where the hour stopped, not off anything she announced.

NO DATED WORK WAS SET IN THIS CLASS AT ALL. No quiz, no test, no Lingco due date, no page assignment, no mention of the 10/13 Test 1. The hour was entirely correction and speaking practice. commitments is empty on purpose.

Then I'm assuming we read drill 6, drill 7 and eight, did we do those?... We did not read 9, right? That's okay, so today we're gonna do 9, 10, 11, and we're gonna also spend some time speaking.' Unit 3 drills 1-11 are now done in class. She named no next drill and no next unit; the ledger plan has unit 3 continuing through the week of 9/21.

off_slide: The whole hour is off-slide by definition - Khouri's slides are never posted, and this class had no deck at all, just the textbook drills, the board, and her voice. Everything below is only in the recording.

The kasra-after-alif fronting rule, which is the single most transferable thing she taught today and is a pronunciation rule the book does not spell out: when the letter after an alif carries a kasra, the alif's vowel moves off 'aa' toward 'e'. She added the sociolinguistic note that the unshifted version is understandable and not wrong, just not native.

The register lesson on Habiibi / Habiibati - not a vocabulary item but a usage rule, that it is reserved for a fiance, a girlfriend, or someone you are serious about, and is not said to a friend of the opposite sex. She had made this point before and repeated it unprompted.

The fuSHa-versus-Shami pairing she keeps running underneath the MSA syllabus: she accepted a student's Levantine word for homework, named it as the Shami one, then asked for the fuSHa one, and separately gave mniiH / mniiHa as the Shami answer to 'how are you' alongside the standard set. This is exactly the two-track vocabulary that only exists in the audio.

The closing culture lesson, prompted by a student asking whether the Levantine 'what's up' opens a conversation or replaces one: the American 'what's up' is a greeting you can say while walking away, whereas 'Arabic culture is more intentional' - seeing someone you know in the street obliges you to stop and give them at least a few minutes, and leaving early requires an apology.

The ellipsis point about spoken versus written Arabic, made in passing but generalisable: 'when we speak, we don't really... we don't care about mentioning every word when we speak. When we write is different. This is in every language.' Hence answering 'how are you' with just the adjective rather than the full sentence is normal, and both are acceptable from them.

Prayer requests opened the class and ran about two and a half minutes: a student getting married in four months in Georgia and returning in the spring with her husband, a student with a heavy homework load, and the SIFA students visiting campus this week. She prayed by name for each.

notes: NOTHING WITH A DATE WAS SAID IN THIS HOUR. No quiz, no test, no Lingco deadline, no reading. Both commitments and assigned_reading are empty because they should be, not because the transcript was thin.

THE HIGH-VALUE CONTENT IS THE ORAL REVIEW BLOCK (roughly 00:34:30-00:44), not the drills. The drills are answer-key delivery for work Parker can do from the book; the review block is Khouri deciding, out loud, which vocabulary she expects to be active, and it is the part with no written source anywhere. Items she chose to pull: hijab, askun fii bayti, waajib / waajibi, kitaab / kitaabi and its masculine-versus-feminine 'your', Habiibi / Habiibati, the full answer set for 'how are you', and haadha / haadhihi.

THE ANSWER SET FOR 'HOW ARE YOU' IS A REAL DISTINCTION SHE DREW AND IT IS EASY TO GET WRONG ON A CARD: bi-khayr is the answer to the GREETING, khayr / al-khayr is 'good' in general. She also required the women to use the feminine adjective form and corrected a student who had used the masculine. And she gave the Shami pair mniiH / mniiHa as an alternative, which fits the pattern that her live vocabulary runs a Levantine track alongside the fuSHa the book teaches.

TRANSCRIPT QUALITY IS THE WORST OF THE FOUR THIS WEEK for a specific reason: this is a language class, so the Arabic is being spoken by beginners, and Teams renders it as English near-homophones. Nothing in the drill segments can be quoted as a word she said. Garbles read through rather than reproduced: 'Habibeti' / 'Happy, Betty' / 'Halibati' for Habiibati; 'Baiti' / 'baby' / 'bad see' for bayti; 'Escon' for askun; 'what zip' / 'Was you be' / 'Well, Zifa' for the homework words; 'the first half' almost certainly for 'the fuSHa one'; 'Massi' for maashi; 'Anna Jayed' for ana jayyid(a); 'lace' / 'Anna Lisa' for lastu; 'the mom' for what follows it; 'Neh / Neha' for mniiH / mniiHa; 'have the / have the he' for haadha / haadhihi; 'Kamsa' for khamsa; 'Teshki' / 'to skill' / 'the skill' / 'dash key' for tashkiil; 'souko' / 'the school' for sukuun; 'regime' / 'gene' / 'the Jo' for jiim; 'the dog' for daal; 'Shufi Mafi' is the one Levantine phrase the captions got close enough to be legible.

TWO PLACES WHERE THE GARBLE SITS EXACTLY ON THE POINT, so no term is asserted: the phrase transcribed 'the Christian, Christian one, order to avoid Allah, Allah's name', offered as one of the answers to 'how are you', could not be resolved and nothing has been attributed to her about it; and the specific fuSHa word for homework is confidently 'waajib' from the shape of the exchange ('what zip' repeated, then 'Was you be' for 'my homework') but the captions never render it cleanly, so it is listed in terms with that caveat rather than quoted.

PACE: unit 3 drills 1-11 are done in class. The ledger plan has unit 3 running through the week of 9/21 and unit 4 starting 9/28, and lectured_through already reads unit 3 - so nothing about the ledger needs to move on today's evidence. She named no next drill.

THE PAIR CONVERSATION IS THE ONE LOOSE END. She set it up and ran out of time before anyone performed. It is recorded as an inferred assignment rather than a commitment because she never said it would resume, never dated it, and never described it as graded - but if it does resume Tuesday, a prepared two-line dialogue using askun fii bayti, the greeting set and haadha is exactly what it would need.

Roughly 2.5 minutes of prayer requests and prayer, 9 minutes on drill 9, 12 on drill 10 at the board, 10 on drill 11, 10 on the oral review, and 4 on the Toyota page and the conversation setup. The drills took 31 of 48 minutes - over-representing reading and writing, and only 10 minutes went to the speaking she says the course is for.
